title: Block C close: the wound and the healing
hook: a split remembered with grief, and a family everyone loves

segments.voice: Yesterday: turbah, hands folded and hands at the sides, one row. Your line was side by side.

It began on the day after. The Prophet ﷺ had died, his body was not yet buried, and the community had to decide who would lead. Then came a pledge in a meeting hall. A pool called Ghadir Khumm. A calendar, a Coptic boy's case, a plague. A caliph killed at home, a battle around a camel, a field called Siffin. Hasan's peace, Husayn's refusal, a river cut off, Zaynab's voice. It's a hard stretch of history, and it has been told two ways. Today the block closes. Today: the wound and the healing.
screen: `A POOL, A CALENDAR, A FIELD, A RIVER.`

segments.voice: Start with the wound. The question of who should lead after the Prophet was answered one way by those who pledged to Abu Bakr, and another way by those who held that the Prophet had named Ali. Out of those answers came the Sunni telling and the Shia telling, and both carried their grief: Uthman killed while reading the Qur'an, Ali struck in the mosque at Kufa, Husayn at Karbala. Neither tradition hides the wound. It is remembered, in sermons and in majalis. Now the healing, which was there all along. The same family is loved on both sides; the blessing on Muhammad and his family is said in prayer by both. The four caliphs and the twelve Imams have one man in common, Ali. The qiblah doesn't move for anyone. And the Qur'an gives words for people who come after an earlier generation. After praising the emigrants and the helpers of Medina, it describes believers who came later and say: "Our Lord! Forgive us and our brethren who were before us in the faith, and place not in our hearts any rancour toward those who believe." That prayer doesn't settle who was right. It asks forgiveness for everyone before us, and a heart without rancor toward everyone now. Read this way, unity isn't an agreement reached. It's something asked for, again and again. Unity is a prayer. Next, the path leaves the split behind and walks into the cities the Muslims built.

If you pray, say the Qur'an's words slowly: Our Lord, forgive us and our brethren who were before us in the faith, and place not in our hearts any rancor toward those who believe. If you don't, bring to mind one rift you know, in a family, a friendship or a community, and hold both sides of it without choosing, breathing in for those who came before and out for those here now.
Ghill, rancor, a grudge in the heart: the word the Qur'an's prayer asks God to remove, closing this block on the wound of the first split and the healing held in common. Today's word.
Your line: unity is a prayer. It doesn't wait for anyone to win the argument. That's a block closed.

howItsDone: Sunni and Shia Muslims remember the early conflicts in different ways, in sermons, histories and Muharram gatherings, and the Qur'an's prayer for 'our brethren who were before us in the faith' (59:10) is recited as a prayer against rancor.

chat.says: After such a painful split, what does the Qur'an teach Muslims to pray?
options: Forgiveness for those before them, and no rancor toward believers now.
That God show the whole world which side of the split was right.
That everyone forget the early history and never speak of it.
chat.meaning: Qur'an 59:10: forgive us and our brethren before us, and place no rancor in our hearts. It asks; it doesn't settle who was right.

Ghadir Khumm.meaning: the pool between Mecca and Medina where the Prophet spoke

Siffin.meaning: the plain where Ali's and Mu'awiyah's armies met

Kufa.meaning: the city in Iraq where Ali was struck in the mosque

majalis.meaning: gatherings to remember Husayn; plural of majlis

Zaynab.meaning: Husayn's sister, who spoke out as a captive
